idiom_name: struct with private fields owning Vec<Child>, mutated through &mut self
implementation_notes: Rust enforces the boundary structurally: everything is private by default (the Reference: 'by default, everything is private'), so `Order { lines, total, .. }` cannot be constructed and `order.lines` cannot be read outside the module; the root owns its `Vec<OrderLine>` by value and a child can only be mutated through a `&mut Order` borrow, which makes two simultaneous mutation paths a compile error. The API guidelines state the design rule directly - public fields 'prevent the type from providing any validation or maintaining any invariants on the contents of the field' - so the root exposes getters returning `&[OrderLine]` and a validating constructor as the only creation path. Other aggregates are referenced by newtype id; persistence is an explicit repository plus transaction (sqlx/diesel), as the standard library has neither - the local idiom (ownership + privacy) replaces the encapsulated-cluster machinery.
pitfalls: A `pub` field, a `pub(crate)` field, or a helper returning `&mut Vec<OrderLine>` hands out mutation rights that bypass the invariant; the compiler helps only as long as the fields stay private.
Interior mutability (`Cell`/`RefCell`/`Mutex`) inside the root moves invariant checks from compile time to run time; prefer `&mut self` methods and let the borrow checker serialize writers.

`#[derive(Clone)]` on the root silently clones the whole cluster - harmless for value-like aggregates, wrong when the identity must stay unique - and `Rc<Customer>` fields would make the aggregate load a foreign boundary and create reference-count cycles.

Serialization/deserialization derives bypass the constructor: `#[derive(Deserialize)]` or a hand-written `FromRow` must validate or route through `new`, otherwise an invalid aggregate can be materialized from data.
